newsitem.title: PERU: Slain Peru rebel chief described as shy, peaceful.
newsitem.headline: Slain Peru rebel chief described as shy, peaceful.

text.p: Eighteen years ago, the intransigence of then 25-year-old Nestor Cerpa Cartolini and other hardline unionists occupying a Lima texile factory led to the deaths of six workers when police stormed the building.
History repeated itself on Tuesday.

This time, Cerpa, 43, and 20-odd Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels were all killed when Peruvian troops stormed the Japanese ambassador's home where they held 72 hostages for more than four months.
One hostage, two soldiers and all 14 guerrillas died in the assault.
Anti-terrorist police described the mastermind of the longest hostage siege in Latin American history as an angry terrorist with a violent past and an unlikely MRTA leader.
But family members and former comrades-in-arms, however, remembered a shy, cautious man committed to leftist revolution but who favoured books over bullets and dialogue over death.
"He's more political than military," said Javier Vela, who fought beside Cerpa in the northern jungle at the height of Peru's guerrilla wars.
"In the bush, he was calm. He never came down into the towns where someone might recognise him. He stayed more with his books -- Marx, Lenin. He always would say 'I hate death.'"

Born into a working class family, Cerpa left school at 17 to find a job. "His father died and he wanted to help the household economically," his mother, Felicita Cartolini, told Reuters Television earlier this year.
"Nestor is an intelligent boy, very capable but non-violent," she said from her home in France, where she lives in "political exile" with Cerpa's two young sons.
In 1977 he joined a group of union leaders organising workers at the Cromotex textile plant.

In a well-planned assault, workers seized the plant, killing one police officer to protest its planned closure and demand back-pay. When police retook it a month later, they killed six workers including Cerpa's mentor, union leader Hemigidio Huertas, and arrested scores of others. Among those severely beaten was Cerpa.
Upon his release 10 months later, Cerpa went underground and helped organise the MRTA in the early 1980s.

"The Cromotex episode marked the life of Nestor Cerpa as it did, in part, that of my family," said Teodosio Gilvonio Conde, whose sister Nancy married Cerpa and is now serving a life sentence for being an MRTA leader.
During his clandestine years, Cerpa took part in a string of attacks on targets ranging from a Catholic church to a Kentucky Fried Chicken outlet, according to police.

A photograph taken during those years depicts a young man with sunglasses and a menacing scowl gripping a machine-gun and standing in front of an MRTA flag. Another shows him with Nancy, their faces covered by neckerchiefs, sitting with a baby. An assault rifle lies on the bed next to the family.
In the early 1990s, Cerpa led guerrilla columns in Peru's northeastern jungle.

Former comrades in the MRTA's one-time stronghold in the Huallaga River valley recalled a careful leader who took pains not to expose himself to capture or gunfire and hid in a house during a fierce battle for the strategic town of Juanjui.

They also remember that he avoided needless cruelty. "He's a very sentimental person, very human. He does not just pull the trigger to annihilate anyone. He exhausts all efforts necessary to avoid that," a former MRTA leader, who asked only to be identified by his nom de guerre "Antonio," told Reuters.

Police sources said Cerpa was largely overshadowed by other rebel leaders and only fell into his role as MRTA chief after his superiors were captured. But the Dec. 17, 1996, takeoover of the residence was brilliantly planned and executed and former hostages attest to Cerpa's intelligence.
"My personal opinion is that he is a cultured man, well-read and quite intelligent," said university professor Carlos Aquino, who was released after five days in captivity.

"I remember Cerpa as a shy man who, despite being in love with Nancy, was incapable of asking her to dance at parties. But when it came to organising the struggle, he was very decisive," said Gilvonio.
